Article Title: Anthropic has committed $50 million to charities in its San Francisco hometown region through 2027; its first $500,000 will support food banks, shelters, hot meals and toys for children, with more gra
Article Text:
Anthropic has committed $50 million to charities in its San Francisco hometown region through 2027; its first $500,000 will support food banks, shelters, hot meals and toys for children, with more grants planned

Which organizations will receive the first grants

Why is Anthropic investing in its hometown

How will $50 million fund work

Anthropic has committed $50 million to nonprofit organisations across the San Francisco Bay Area, with grants expected to reach local community groups by the end of 2027. The AI company said the funding will be managed through a donor advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation, with its first $500,000 being distributed immediately to four organisations. The initial grants will support food access, free community meals, winter shelter services and a toy programme for children facing difficult circumstances. The partnership focuses particularly on San Francisco, Anthropic’s hometown, where the company says it hopes to expand opportunity and strengthen local communities in the region.As announced by the company, the first $500,000 will go to four organisations supporting communities across San Francisco and nearby areas. SF-Marin Food Bank partners with 265 community organisations across two counties to help families access fresh, healthy food.GLIDE, a Tenderloin-based organisation, provides three free meals a day, 364 days a year. It also supports families as they pursue health, stable homes and opportunity. The Interfaith Winter Shelter, founded by the San Francisco Interfaith Council, has brought together more than 50 faith communities for over three decades.It provides people experiencing homelessness with a warm bed, a hot meal and a shower.San Francisco Firefighters Local 798 Toy Program, run by active and retired firefighters since 1949, provides toys to children facing difficult circumstances, including those recovering from fires or disasters, or living in family shelters, hospital wards or protective custody.San Francisco has been home to Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei since childhood. Both attended Lowell High School before starting the AI company in their hometown. Early employees also gathered at Precita Park to map out a vision for safer AI systems.Anthropic now has more than 2,500 employees at its San Francisco headquarters. Its Claude chatbot is also widely used by local businesses and nonprofits.Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic, said:“San Francisco has always been a place of enormous possibility, but that possibility isn’t shared equally by everyone. We have been privileged to build Anthropic here, and we want to make sure our success expands opportunity, not widens the gaps that already exist. That’s why we’re partnering with the San Francisco Foundation, whose deep knowledge of the Bay Area will help guide this commitment to where it’s needed most,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.Anthropic has established a donor advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation (SFF) to draw on the foundation’s local knowledge and direct support towards community needs. A donor advised fund is a charitable fund set aside for giving. The donor contributes money and recommends nonprofit organisations to support, while the foundation manages the details and brings its local expertise to the recommendations.SFF is a community foundation that works with donors, nonprofits and neighbours to pool resources and direct them towards regional priorities. Anthropic said it will draw on SFF’s nearly 80 years of knowledge and expertise as it determines the fund’s grant recipients.Fred Blackwell, CEO of the San Francisco Foundation, said:“Where you live matters, and so does what you put into it. The Bay Area has always been a place where people build big things. That should include building strong communities. Anthropic is making a real commitment to the place it calls home, and we hope others are inspired to do the same. That’s how the whole region thrives,” said Fred Blackwell, CEO, San Francisco Foundation.
Article Summary: Anthropic has committed $50 million to charities in its San Francisco hometown region through 2027. Its first $500,000 will support food banks, shelters, hot meals and toys for children, with more grants planned. The AI company said the funding will be managed through a donor advised fund at the San Francisco Foundation.

Article Title: In 2025, Jensen Huang backed nepotism saying it doesn't bother him: ‘Many Nvidia second-generation employees even…’
Article Text:
Jensen Huang

A rare family presence in Silicon Valley

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently admitted to having an extramarital affair and soon after his admission, talks surrounding succession at Nvidia have gained momentum. Amid this, an older report has resurfaced in which Huang defended nepotism during a recent company all-hands meeting, claiming that employees' children often end up doing a better job than their parents. Speaking at a recent all-hands meeting last year, Huang acknowledged that many staff members’ children work at the company and insisted it doesn't bother him. He reasoned that parents wouldn't recommend their own kids for a job if they thought they would embarrass them – and added with a smile that many “Nvidia second-generation” employees even outperform their parents.The comments come as Nvidia faces closer attention over its hiring practices, particularly because Huang’s own children, Madison and Spencer, have moved into key roles within the company’s emerging business divisions.However, Nvidia has no public succession plan and no obvious heir. Huang holds both the CEO and president titles. Under him, Nvidia has taken an estimated 90% of the market for the chips behind large Al projects. According to a report, Huang has long rejected conventional hierarchy and once said on a podcast that traditional organisational charts made no sense to him. He runs Nvidia mostly through project meetings that bring together recent graduates and senior executives in the same room.Having multiple generations under one roof is unusual for Silicon Valley, where the children of tech pioneers like Apple's Steve Jobs and Microsoft’s Bill Gates typically steered clear of their parents' companies. At Nvidia, however, the family ties extend beyond the CEO. Children of co-founder Chris Malachowsky and Director Aarti Shah also work at the firm.Rather than working in Nvidia’s core chip and data center business, Huang's children have carved out spots in newer, future-focused areas. Madison Huang leads the Omniverse department, focusing on 3D simulation and Digital Twin software. Spencer Huang concentrates on AI models and developing robotics perception software.Madison’s rapid rise at Nvidia has drawn plenty of attention across the tech industry. Just four years after joining the company, she is part of her father's core leadership team, with a 2023 compensation package that topped $1 million. Spencer, meanwhile, has taken a quieter approach, working behind the scenes on Nvidia’s robotics goals while avoiding the spotlight.Former Nvidia Vice President Greg Estes acknowledged the family connection, emphasising that both siblings “work very hard, excel in their respective fields, and have a deep attachment to the company.”
Article Summary: Jensen Huang defended nepotism during a recent company all-hands meeting. Said employees' children often end up doing a better job than their parents. Comments come as Nvidia faces closer attention over its hiring practices. Huang’s own children, Madison and Spencer, have moved into key roles.

Article Title: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon on the ‘one of the biggest threats’ to CEOs career and their company’s success
Article Text:
JP Morgan CEO Jamie Dimon

Jamie Dimon on why criticism matters more than ego

Jamie Dimon's ‘Ted Lasso’ approach to leadership

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has spent more than 20 years at the top of the banking world, and he has a clear view of what separates great leaders from the ones who fail. According to him, it has very little to do with how much an executive actually knows about business. Dimon has identified insecurity as one of the biggest threats to both a CEO’s career and their company’s success. The problem often starts with a promotion – as executives climb the corporate ladder, they shift from being experts in one specific area to generalists overseeing parts of the business they barely know.“The bigger job you get, the less you know—literally—about the job,” Dimon said on the Master Investor Podcast earlier this year. Strong CEOs handle this shift by hiring people who know more than they do, without feeling embarrassed about their own blind spots. Insecure leaders, on the other hand, try to hide what they don’t know. “It becomes PowerPoints, you know, make them look good, don’t tell them the bad news. And that is what causes the problem,” Dimon said (Fortune reported).Dimon argued that this kind of insecurity is actually a deeper leadership flaw than arrogance, and it creates a ripple effect of other problems.In his view, a CEO has to be able to take criticism – especially when it comes from unhappy customers – and use it to fix what is broken.“You’re not going to hurt my feelings by telling me we have a crappy product. If you’re right, I’m gonna thank you for letting me know,” he said.In an October interview with the Wall Street Journal, Dimon pointed to an unlikely role model for upper management: Ted Lasso, the relentlessly positive fictional soccer coach from the Apple TV series. Dimon said Lasso nails the balance between two essential leadership traits: a fierce drive to win, paired with genuine empathy and humility.“I love Ted Lasso. He comes in and he doesn’t know anything about football, and he’s just gracious. He’s working with people – their insecurities, their bad behavior, their work ethic – and he’s getting them to function as a team,” Dimon said.Dimon’s views on leadership carry weight because of his results. Over the past two decades, he has built JPMorgan Chase into an $894 billion banking giant – the largest US bank by market cap.
Article Summary: JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has spent more than 20 years at the top of the banking world. Dimon says insecurity is one of the biggest threats to both a CEO's career and their company's success. He points to Ted Lasso, the relentlessly positive fictional soccer coach from the Apple TV series as a role model.

Article Title: Deal to create world's biggest electricity company, worth $67 billion, is in trouble; residents fear it will...
Article Text:
Rising power bills put $67 billion merger at risk (Picture: NextEra Energy)

Virginia wants a rate freeze, NextEra is saying no

Virginians are paying over 10% more for electricity than a year ago

A $67 billion deal that would create the world's largest retail electricity company is running into fierce resistance in Virginia. Florida-based NextEra Energy wants to buy Richmond-headquartered Dominion Energy, but the state's governor, its attorney general and a growing number of residents say the merger offers Virginians too little and could push their power bills even higher.The fight comes as electricity prices climb across the US, driven partly by the power demand of AI data centres. Virginia is where that boom is most visible. Dominion, which has 3.6 million customers across three states, serves Northern Virginia's Data Center Alley, the world's largest cluster of such facilities. The State Corporation Commission (SCC), which must approve the deal, is set to rule in January, and needs two of its three commissioners on board.Governor Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, wants electricity rates frozen for six years and bill credits of $29 a month for four years for current Dominion customers. "My priority is affordability for Virginians," she told reporters ahead of a public hearing last week, The New York Times reported.NextEra's offer is much smaller: $10 a month in credits for four years, plus $100 million for bill assistance to lower-income households and workforce programmes.In a filing this week, chief executive John Ketchum rejected the freeze, saying it should be handled in routine rate-setting cases rather than the merger review.The companies have tried to narrow the gap. Earlier this month, they accepted 101 of 117 conditions proposed by the SCC staff and the state's consumer counsel, including two independent directors on the Virginia utility's board and up to $5 billion in spending with local businesses over five years. They still refused the freeze and a staff proposal for a three-year rate cap.Wall Street has noticed the standoff. The premium on NextEra's all-stock offer has shrunk from 23% in May to under 2%.US Energy Information Administration figures cited by the NYT show Virginians paid an average of $176 a month in August for 1,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, up from $159 a year earlier. The national average rose from $176 to $182.That strain was on display outside the SCC hearing in Richmond, where dozens of protesters, several of them local pastors, held signs reading "Take Back Our Power." The Rev. Kevin L. Jones of Ebenezer Baptist Church told the NYT that requests from parishioners for help with utility bills now add up to thousands of dollars.Critics have also questioned the SCC's own neutrality. Its chair, Judge Kelsey A. Bagot, was a senior attorney at NextEra less than three years ago. She has declined to recuse herself, arguing that past work with a regulated company has never automatically required a commissioner to step aside.The deal does have backers. Virginia Chamber of Commerce chief Brad N. Hall told the commission the merger would bring more investment into the grid and help build the state's workforce. Still, the SCC staff and the independent monitor for the regional grid have joined the governor and attorney general in opposing it.Even a yes in Richmond would not settle things. The deal also needs clearance from North Carolina, South Carolina and federal regulators. NextEra has tried to buy utilities in Hawaii, North Carolina and Texas before, and each bid fell apart. January will show whether Virginia joins that list.
Article Summary: Florida-based NextEra Energy wants to buy Richmond-headquartered Dominion Energy. Virginia's governor, its attorney general and a growing number of residents say the merger offers Virginians too little and could push their power bills even higher. The fight comes as electricity prices climb across the US, driven partly by the power demand of AI data centres.

Article Title: FBI warns of Europe-like freezer hacking attacks in Walmart, Target and other US supermarkets: 6 things the agency wants these retailers to do
Article Text:
FBI warning on freezer attacks

Read FBI cyber branch’s warning

The @FBI and our partners are seeing malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems around the world. These systems help keep food, medicine, and other products at safe temperatures and are widely used across critical infrastructure sectors.

Attackers are targeting electronic temperature and refrigeration controllers, particularly in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. In at least one recent incident, attackers targeted refrigeration components at three foreign blood service facilities.

While this attack was unsuccessful due to the proper alert mechanisms in place, security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings, potentially causing inventory loss and equipment damage

Potential links to US military base incidents

6 things the FBI wants companies to do

Take controllers off the public internet

Put access behind a firewall

Change default passwords

Learn how vendors configure devices

Set safe temperature limits

Ensure alerts reach the right contacts

The FBI has warned American grocery stores and cold storage facilities to lock down their refrigeration systems, following a wave of cyberattacks in Europe where hackers remotely raised freezer temperatures and ruined store inventories. In a post on X (formerly Twitter) by the FBI Cyber Branch, the agency said it is tracking malicious cyber activity targeting industrial refrigeration and cold-chain monitoring systems worldwide. These electronic controllers are used across critical infrastructure to keep food, medicine and other temperature-sensitive goods safe.The warning comes just days after supermarkets in France, Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit by remote hackers who raised fridge and freezer temperatures, forcing stores to throw out spoiled food. Hackers also recently targeted refrigeration components at three foreign blood service facilities – an attack that failed only because proper alert systems were in place.Security experts and federal investigators are looking closely at whether similar attacks have already reached American soil. In August, a series of freezer malfunctions ruined food at six US military base commissaries.Those incidents are currently under investigation as a suspected hack. The Army Criminal Investigation Division’s Cyber Field Office, the Defense Commissary Agency, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service – all operating under the US Department of Defense – are working with French law enforcement to determine if the military base malfunctions are connected to the European grocery store attacks.In an accompanying video message, Brett Leatherman, Assistant Director of the FBI Cyber Division, explained how attackers are breaking in.“These systems protect food and medicine across healthcare, food and agriculture, and other critical sectors here in the United States as well. Attackers are getting in through controllers that are unpatched, reachable from the internet, or still using the default passwords listed in the manufacturer’s manual,” Leatherman said, New York Post reported.Once inside, hackers can alter system settings, leading to spoiled inventory and damaged equipment. To prevent this, the FBI is urging organisations to take six specific steps:

Security weaknesses in unpatched or internet-accessible controllers can allow attackers to change system settings. The warning comes just days after supermarkets in France, Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg and Estonia were hit by remote hackers.

Article Title: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's 'common sense regulation' loses support of Democratic New York City Councilman in the fear that it may make 'unhappy' Amazon go for ...
Article Text:
What the bill does

Amazon warns of warehouse closures

Pressure on council members

Menin under pressure to schedule a vote

Legal questions also under review

A New York City Democratic councilman has withdrawn his support for a controversial labour bill backed by Mayor Zohran Mamdani, citing concerns that the measure could lead to business closures and significant job losses, according to a report by the New York Post. Queens Councilman Phil Wong recently removed his name as a co-sponsor of the Delivery Protection Act after meeting with small business owners and logistics operators who warned that the legislation could have serious economic consequences. The bill, introduced by fellow Queens Democrat Tiffany Cabán, seeks to overhaul employment practices for "last-mile" delivery workers by requiring companies such as Amazon to directly employ delivery drivers rather than relying on subcontractors.“I’ve been talking to many of the small businesses,” Wong told the New York Post. “If this bill gets passed, it will close a lot of them and that’s bad for my district.”Councilwoman Tiffany Cabán introduced the bill in 2025, and Wong signed on as a co-sponsor. After she reintroduced it this year, he supported it again. The legislation would end Amazon’s reliance on subcontractors by requiring it to obtain licences for its 15 last-mile facilities in the city and to hire delivery workers directly as full-time employees.Other companies, including FedEx, would face the same rules. According to Amazon, the bill would affect more than 5,000 delivery workers employed by about 40 third-party contractors. Amazon doesn’t directly employ delivery drivers anywhere in the US. It has threatened to close its New York last-mile warehouses and lay off about 2,000 workers there if the bill passes. An AKFR study commissioned by Amazon estimates that delivery costs for New Yorkers would rise by $664 a year, or about $5.20 a package.The Teamsters union, which strongly backs the bill, accuses Amazon of union-busting and of using the subcontracting model to dodge responsibility for worker and street safety. The union says Amazon has spent more than $5 million on a campaign against the bill.Amazon has strongly opposed the bill and has warned that it could shut down its last-mile warehouses in New York City if the legislation becomes law. The company has said such a move could result in the loss of about 2,000 warehouse jobs. The e-commerce giant also argues that consumers could face higher costs. A study commissioned by Amazon and conducted by AKFR estimated that New Yorkers' delivery costs could rise by an average of $664 annually, or roughly $5.20 per package, if the proposal is enacted.One unnamed council member who supports the bill's objectives but remains concerned about its consequences told the Post that many lawmakers may not fully understand the proposal's impact.“I agree with the intent of the bill to protect workers, but I’m concerned about people losing their jobs and the sponsor doesn’t deny that people will lose their jobs,” the council member said.One of the bill’s 35 current co-sponsors, who asked not to be named, told the Post there is “tremendous political pressure” and that many colleagues, including the speaker, don’t fully understand the bill’s ramifications. The member agreed with its intent to protect workers but said the sponsor doesn’t deny that jobs will be lost. Wong’s chief of staff, Daniel Kurzyna, said the Teamsters called his office within minutes of the name being removed in September. “They noticed fast,” he said, adding that the union has called regularly since asking Wong to reconsider.Rep. Ro Khanna, a California Democrat who is considering a 2028 presidential run, urged Council Speaker Julie Menin to schedule a vote, writing on X that delivery workers deserve safe and fair conditions. Menin, a centrist, has not taken a position on the bill. She has voiced concern that it could cause job losses and lead Amazon to raise prices. Mamdani and Teamsters members rallied at City Hall on October 22, urging her to call a vote immediately. Menin says the bill is being reviewed by the city’s Law Department, according to a spokesperson, who said she remains committed to legislation that protects workers and keeps the jobs in New York. Sources told the Post the Law Department is examining whether the bill violates the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994, which bars states from regulating the price, route or service of motor carriers. New York would be the first US city to adopt such a measure.Beyond the political debate, the bill faces legal scrutiny. According to the New York Post report, New York City's Law Department is examining whether the proposal could conflict with the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994, which limits states and local governments from enacting regulations related to the prices, routes or services of motor carriers. Speaker Julie Menin has not publicly endorsed or opposed the legislation but has expressed concerns that it could lead to job losses and higher costs for consumers. Her office said the bill remains under review and continues to move through the legislative process.The latest development highlights growing divisions within New York City's Democratic leadership as officials weigh worker protections against warnings from businesses that stricter regulations could prompt companies such as Amazon to scale back operations in the city.
Article Summary: Queens Councilman Phil Wong removed his name as a co-sponsor of the Delivery Protection Act. The bill seeks to overhaul employment practices for "last-mile" delivery workers. It would require companies such as Amazon to directly employ delivery drivers rather than relying on subcontractors. Amazon has warned that it could shut down its last-mile warehouses in New York City if the legislation becomes law.

Article Title: Meta’s chief strategy officer Dave Wehner is leaving the company for four-year-old AI startup; sends 'right mission' message; says: I have become increasingly ...
Article Text:
From Meta veteran to AI challenger

Fireworks eyes its next phase of growth

AI boom draws senior executives

AI race intensifies

Read Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner’s complete post here

Wehner's move underscores the growing pull of the AI industry as startups compete with larger rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and major cloud providers.

With fresh capital, rising valuations and growing enterprise demand for AI infrastructure, companies like Fireworks are increasingly attracting experienced leaders who see artificial intelligence as the next major technology platform.

Read Meta chief strategy officer Dave Wehner’s complete post here

I announced earlier this week that I am leaving Meta. I am deeply grateful to Mark Zuckerberg for showing what a truly founder-led company can achieve.

I am incredibly optimistic for Meta’s future.

At Meta, I was able to witness the most exciting opportunities in enterprise AI. That’s why today, I’m announcing that I will be joining Fireworks as CFO. I am thrilled to be joining a founder-led growth company where I can roll up my sleeves and put my experience to work.

Fireworks has the right mission for the moment. Companies will use AI to build on what makes them distinctive: their data and expertise.

Specialized intelligence gives them a way to capture those advantages and own their “alpha.” Open models offer price points that allow the technology to have the greatest impact. Fireworks is building the platform to make all of this possible.

I’ve known and respected Lin

for a long time. As I’ve spent more time with her and the people at Fireworks, I’ve become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There’s a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need.

I see AI as the most consequential technology shift of my lifetime. I’m excited to get to work and help build a business at the center of it.

Dave Wehner, Meta’s chief strategy officer and former chief financial officer, is leaving the social media giant to join fast-growing AI startup Lin Qiao-led Fireworks as its new CFO, marking another high-profile move from Big Tech into the artificial intelligence sector. Wehner announced the move in a post on X, saying he had become increasingly convinced of the opportunity ahead for the four-year-old startup. “Fireworks has the right mission for the moment,” he wrote. “I’ve become increasingly bullish on what they are building. There’s a remarkable depth of technical talent here, coupled with a very practical focus on what customers need.” Fireworks, which provides AI inference and model-training services built around open-source AI models, was valued at $17.5 billion in a Series D funding round in July.Wehner joined Meta, then known as Facebook, in 2012 and served as the company’s chief financial officer from 2014 to 2022 before taking on the role of chief strategy officer. During his tenure, he helped steer the company through a period of rapid growth, expanding advertising revenues and major bets on new technologies. In a statement to CNBC, Meta COO Javier Olivan praised Wehner's contributions, saying he helped guide the company through “tremendous growth and complexity” over the past 14 years while bringing disciplined thinking to some of its most important strategic decisions.At Fireworks, Wehner will oversee the company's finances and operations as it looks to scale further in the increasingly competitive AI market. CEO Lin Qiao said Wehner's experience would help the company as it enters its next stage of expansion.Founded in 2022 by former Meta and Google employees, Fireworks allows developers and businesses to customise, train and run open AI models. The company counts investors such as Nvidia and Sequoia Capital among its backers and has reportedly held early discussions for another funding round that could value the startup between $30 billion and $40 billion.“Dave told me he wanted to get back to a smaller company where he could build toward a big impact again,” Qiao wrote in a LinkedIn post. “He sees AI as the defining technology shift of his lifetime and wants to help shape what comes next.”Wehner's departure comes as venture-backed AI companies continue to attract seasoned executives from some of the world's largest technology firms. While Fireworks remains significantly smaller than Meta, which had a market capitalisation of about $1.56 trillion at Friday's close, the startup is positioning itself as a key player in the market for open AI models.The company has also faced challenges associated with rapid growth. In October, Fireworks disclosed a security incident involving unauthorised use of internal credentials that allowed limited access to environment variables used in evaluation jobs within a small number of customer accounts. The company said its investigation found no evidence of unauthorised access to customer models, datasets, training data, personal information or inference traffic.Wehner's move underscores the growing pull of the AI industry as startups compete with larger rivals such as OpenAI, Anthropic and major cloud providers. With fresh capital, rising valuations and growing enterprise demand for AI infrastructure, companies like Fireworks are increasingly attracting experienced leaders who see artificial intelligence as the next major technology platform.
Article Summary: Dave Wehner, Meta’s chief strategy officer and former chief financial officer, is leaving the social media giant to join fast-growing AI startup Fireworks. Wehner announced the move in a post on X, saying he had become increasingly convinced of the opportunity ahead for the four-year-old startup. Fireworks provides AI inference and model-training services built around open-source AI models.

Article Title: Meta expands AI age checks on Instagram to protect millions more teens worldwide
Article Text:
Meta expands AI age checks on Instagram to protect millions more teens worldwide

How Meta’s AI technology identifies teen users

Parents in the US will receive Instagram notifications

Meta begins using Apple’s age-range signal in Australia

Meta has expanded its AI age-estimation technology globally to place millions more teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. As announced by the company, starting this month, parents in the United States will begin receiving a notification on Instagram explaining how we place teens in age-appropriate protections, and how they can help make sure their teen’s age is accurate. Meta said that the move will bring millions more teens worldwide under Instagram’s Teen Account safeguards. The technology is designed to identify users who may be between 13 and 17 years old based on signals that suggest their age, rather than relying only on the birthday they provide.Meta said it uses AI to find accounts that it suspects belong to teenagers, even when users have misrepresented their age. Once identified, these accounts are placed in Teen Account protections. These safeguards automatically limit who can contact teens, the content they can see and the amount of time they spend on the platform. Teen Accounts are available across Instagram, Facebook and Messenger.Meta said it has been using the technology to place more teens into age-appropriate experiences and is now expanding it globally based on the results so far.The company is also continuing to roll out the technology on Facebook.It plans to begin launching similar age-estimation technology globally on Threads later this year.Meta is also introducing a new way to inform parents about its age-assurance measures. Starting this month, parents in the United States will begin seeing an in-feed video on Instagram explaining how the platform determines whether teens are receiving age-appropriate protections. The video will link to an article outlining Meta’s approach and how parents can help ensure their children have provided the correct age.The article, written by internet safety advocate Larry Magid, will be available to parents worldwide.Meta said its approach involves multiple layers, including efforts to keep children under 13 off its platforms, provide age-appropriate experiences for teenagers and help parents understand how they can support accurate age information.In Australia, Meta has started using Apple’s age-range signal as an additional way to determine a user’s age. Under the process, parents setting up a smartphone for their teen can choose to have the app store confirm the user’s age range. When the teen downloads an app, Apple can share that age-range signal with the developer, helping the app determine whether the user meets its age requirements.Meta said it is voluntarily using the signal. However, it argued that protections could remain inconsistent across apps as long as app stores and developers are not required to participate.The company has supported legislation that would require age verification and parental consent at the app-store level. Meta said a single verified age signal shared consistently with apps could be more effective and privacy-preserving than requiring every platform to conduct its own age checks.
Article Summary: Meta has expanded its AI age-estimation technology globally to place millions more teens in Teen Account protections on Instagram. The technology is designed to identify users who may be between 13 and 17 years old based on signals that suggest their age, rather than relying only on the birthday they provide. Starting this month, parents in the US will begin receiving a notification on Instagram explaining how we place teens in age-appropriate protections.

Article Title: FDA warns against popular anti-obesity drugs; including the one Elon Musk publicly admitted taking for weight loss and said that they can improve quality of life for Americans
Article Text:
FDA warns against popular anti-obesity drugs; including the one Elon Musk publicly admitted taking for weight loss and said that they can improve quality of life for Americans

What is the condition FDA has warned about

When Elon Musk admitted taking anti-obesity drug

What FDA data says

America's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is warning that popular obesity drugs, including Ozempic, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Mounjaro, may carry a "potential increased risk" of a rare eye condition that can lead to permanent vision loss. For those unaware, Mounjaro, Ozempic and Wegovy are all part of a buzzy class of drugs known as GLP-1 agonists, which are seen as potential game-changers for patients struggling with obesity and diabetes.In a recent drug safety communication, the FDA said that it will now require makers of GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs to add a warning about that risk on their drug labels. As per the advisory, "The US Food and Drug Administration is informing patients and health care providers of a potential increased risk of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION) associated with use of glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 RA) medications. NAION is a rare condition that can result in acute, painless, decreased vision in one eye, including permanent vision loss."It’s unknown how GLP-1 drugs may cause NAION. The condition is rare overall, occurring in somewhere between two and 10 people in 100,000 in the general population, according to the American Academy of Ophthalmology. These small numbers have reportedly made it more difficult to determine with certainty if there is a connection.Further complicating the potential link is the fact that the risk factors for developing NAION are common among patients taking GLP-1 drugs. The risk factors include diabetes, cardiovascular disease, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, metabolic syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea.In December 2024, Elon Musk showed off a trimmer figure in a holiday social media post while revealing that he has been taking an anti-obesity drug to shed weight. Tesla CEO posted a photo of himself on Twitter on Christmas Day dressed up in a Santa costume, captioning the picture, "Ozempic Santa." He added, "Technically, Mounjaro, but that doesn't have the same ring to it."A few days earlier in another post on these medicines, Musk wrote, "Nothing would do more to improve the health, lifespan and quality of life for Americans than making GLP inhibitors super low cost to the public. Nothing else is even close."In July 2024, Hathaway et al. published an article titled “Risk of Nonarteritic Anterior Ischemic Optic Neuropathy in Patients Prescribed Semaglutide.”[1] Although FDA identified several limitations of this study, the agency determined that further assessment of the potential increased risk for NAION was warranted. Therefore, FDA undertook a comprehensive evaluation of clinical trial data, animal data, and postmarketing data, including observational studies and case reports.FDA conducted a detailed review of reports of NAION in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs that were received through the FDA Adverse Event Monitoring System (AEMS), formerly the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS). These reports were challenging to interpret because the risk factors for NAION often overlap with conditions common in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs. Therefore, FDA evaluated other data sources, described below, to further assess for a potential relationship between GLP-1 RA use and NAION.FDA review of the available animal data did not identify a mechanism for how GLP-1 RA use could increase the potential risk of NAION.FDA performed a meta-analysis of clinical trials across GLP-1 RA development programs because of the small number or absence of cases of NAION observed in individual trials. The primary objective of the meta-analysis was to assess the incidence of NAION events in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs compared to the incidence in patients treated with a comparator (a placebo or a non-GLP-1 RA glucose-lowering medication). There were 126 such trials for GLP-1 RAs included in the meta-analysis, including a total of 134,253 patients (78,217 GLP-1 RA users and 56,036 patients receiving a comparator) with 288,879 PY of exposure (156,947 PY for the GLP-1 RA users and 131,932 PY for the patients receiving a comparator). We identified 15 probable NAION events, 10 in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs, 5 in patients receiving placebo, and none in patients who received other non-GLP-1 RA glucose-lowering medication. Overall, the results showed a NAION incidence rate of 6.4 events per 100,000 PY in patients treated with GLP-1 RAs compared to 3.8 events per 100,000 PY in comparator-treated patients.
Article Summary: Mounjaro, Ozempic and Wegovy are all part of a buzzy class of drugs known as GLP-1 agonists. FDA said it will now require makers of these drugs to add a warning on their drug labels.

Article Title: Buying screenless tracker over smartwatch: Here's what you get and what you may miss
Article Text:
What a screenless tracker offers

Where a screenless tracker wins

Where screenless tracker falls short

What a smartwatch offers

Where smartwatch wins

Where smartwatch falls short

Screenless tracker Smartwatch Battery life Longer 18 to 36 hours on many full-featured models Distractions None Alerts and pings Live workout stats Not available without your phone On your wrist Sleep comfort Slim and lightweight Can feel bulky Daily utility No timers, alarms or call alerts Calls, texts, calendar alerts, payments

Which one should you choose?

Picking a fitness wearable is no longer just a question of which brand to buy. Today, you also have to decide whether you want a screen on your wrist or not at all. On one side is the screenless tracker, a slim, lightweight device that quietly collects data, and the form factor has gained popularity in recent months. Recently, Whoop, Google (Fitbit Air), Noise and other companies have launched these discrete fitness trackers.On the other hand is the smartwatch, which works as an extension of your smartphone while tracking your daily activity. Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4, Samsung Galaxy Ultra 2 and Galaxy Watch 9, and Google Pixel Watch 5 are some of the flagship products in the market. Both can help you keep an eye on your health, but they suit very different lifestyles. Here is a clear look at what you gain and what you give up with each one.A screenless tracker does exactly what the name suggests. There is no display, so there is nothing to light up, buzz or ping while you go about your day. The device simply collects data and you look at it later on a smartphone app. For people tired of constant alerts, that can be a big relief.No digital distractions. As there are no notifications, buzzes or bright displays, nothing interrupts a conversation and nothing lights up at bedtime.You stay present with the people around you.Another advantage is that these screenless trackers have longer battery life. A screen uses a lot of power. Without one, these devices run anywhere from 5 days to a full month on a single charge. That means far fewer trips to the charger.Thirdly, higher comfort, all day and night. The slim and lightweight design makes a screenless tracker much easier to wear around the clock, especially while sleeping.Moreover, a screenless tracker allows you to flaunt your favourite wrist watch, so you get freedom to keep wearing your classic analog or luxury mechanical watch on your wrist.No real-time workout stats. This means that you cannot check your live pace, elapsed time or heart-rate zones during a workout without pulling out your phone. For runners and gym-goers who like to adjust their effort on the go, this is a drawback.The second thing is there is no daily utility for those who lean towards smartwatches. Screenless trackers will not get quick timers, alarms, step displays or incoming call alerts.Smartwatches, such as the Apple Watch, Wear OS models like the offerings from Samsung and Google, and other models including Amazfit, act as an extension of your smartphone while tracking your daily activity. They put information and controls right on your wrist.The first advantage is instant glanceability. You can check pace, heart rate, timers and rep counts mid-workout with a quick look at your wrist.There is also day-to-day convenience. A smartwatch lets you take calls, reply to quick texts, check calendar alerts and, in some countries, pay at checkout counters – all without reaching for your phone.Thirdly, standalone navigation and audio. Many models support built-in GPS and offline music storage. That means you can leave your phone at home for outdoor runs.One of the drawbacks is frequent charging. Many full-featured smartwatches last about a day or two, which forces regular top-ups. Those charging breaks can disrupt continuous sleep tracking.Some people have constant screen distractions. Alerts and pings can be disruptive while you're working out, working or resting.Lastly, the rigid casing and glass screen can feel intrusive or uncomfortable to sleep in.Quick comparisonChoose a screenless tracker if you want a device that stays out of your way. It suits people who want fewer digital distractions, a slim and lightweight device to sleep in and a battery that needs charging only once every few days. It also works well if you love your analog or mechanical watch and do not want to give it up.Choose a smartwatch if you want information and tools on your wrist. It is the better fit if you like to see your pace and heart rate mid-workout, handle calls and quick texts, pay at checkout counters, or head out for outdoor runs without your phone. In return, you will need to charge it often, and its screen will keep competing for your attention.
Article Summary: Screenless trackers do exactly what the name suggests. There is no display, so there is nothing to light up, buzz or ping while you go about your day. Smartwatches act as an extension of your smartphone while tracking your daily activity. They put information and controls right on your wrist.

Article Title: US air traffic control still runs on floppy disks; Transportation Secretary says: The greatest nation in the world deserves a...
Article Text:
Floppy disks are out of US airports by 2028

Floppy-era systems still deliver weather alerts and NOTAMs to US controllers

The FAA's floppy disk exit has been six years and two administrations in the making

The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is finally pulling floppy disks out of its air traffic control system. The agency has announced that the ageing information display systems used by controllers, some of which still load weather updates and pilot reports from 3.5-inch disks, will be replaced by a new platform called the Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS). The switch will reach 435 facilities across the country and is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2028.Atlantic City International Airport, Nashville International Airport and Greater Rochester International Airport in New York will be the first to get E-IDS, along with data processing hubs in Atlanta and Salt Lake City. US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who credited President Trump for the overhaul, said, "The greatest nation in the world deserves a state-of-the-art air traffic control system." He also put it more bluntly: "Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in. "E-IDS will replace four legacy tools: IDS-4, ACE-IDS, NIDS and ERIDS. The oldest of these, IDS-4, runs on MS-DOS and has been in constant use since the early 1990s on desktop PCs fitted with floppy drives. A 3.5-inch disk holds 1.44MB of data, which is less than a single photo from most smartphones today.What sits on those screens is far from trivial. Controllers use them to read pilot reports on weather conditions (PIREPs), Notices to Airmen (NOTAMs) that flag hazards and restricted airspace, approach charts and airport status.Much of it is still updated by hand. A US Government Accountability Office report from September called the legacy systems cumbersome to search, pointing to interfaces from the 1980s and manual update methods.E-IDS brings all of this into a single view. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said it will let controllers "instantly share critical flight alerts, restricted airspace schedules and pilot reports" across the National Airspace System.The groundwork predates the current administration. The FAA awarded the E-IDS design contract to Leidos in August 2020 as part of its NextGen modernisation programme, which goes back to 2008, and the project carried on through the Biden years. The push picked up pace after the January 2025 midair collision between a passenger jet and an Army helicopter near Washington, when officials noted that flights were still tracked on paper strips and some computers ran Windows 95.The FAA is not the only government body that held on to floppies. The Pentagon used 8-inch disks in its nuclear command and control system until 2019, and Japan scrapped rules requiring floppy disks for some government filings only in 2024.For now, controllers at most US facilities will keep sliding disks into drives until their turn comes. The last of the 435 sites is due to make the move in two years.
Article Summary: The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) is finally pulling floppy disks out of its air traffic control system. The agency has announced that the ageing information display systems used by controllers will be replaced by a new platform called the Enterprise Information Display System (E-IDS) The switch will reach 435 facilities across the country and is scheduled to be completed by the end of 2028.

Article Title: America's datacentre buildout is hurting Japanese giant Softbank, as the company reports $7 billion net loss; but remains optimist as CFO Yoshimitsu Goto sees much promise in …
Article Text:
America's datacentre buildout is hurting Japanese giant Softbank, as the company reports $7 billion net loss; but remains optimist as CFO Yoshimitsu Goto sees much promise in …

Softbank’s AI borrowing becomes a concern for investors

Softbank has reported a $7 billion quarterly loss because of hefty buildout costs for data centres in the US and increases in financing payments, reports Reuters. The Japanese investment giant raised $56.5 billion during the July-September quarter, its highest ever quarterly total as founder Masayoshi Son continues to invest aggressively in AI. The company said it logged a $3.7 billion loss due to advance payments for equipment in US data centre projects after plans changed. The company expects these losses to be offset by rebates for future purchases and said that it will be entitled to rebates of up to $2.1 billion on future purchases.However, Softbank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto remains optimistic stating that data centre projects, which include a large-scale development in Pike County, Ohio, hold much promise.“These data centre projects have only just begun, and we expect that over the next five or 10 years, they will grow further and become much larger in scale,” he ​told a press briefing as stated in the report.As mentioned above, Softbank reported a quarterly loss of 1.1 trillion yen ($7 billion) far exceeding analysts' forecasts and ​comparing with a 2.5 trillion yen profit in the same period a year earlier. The quarterly results, as the report says, is expected to intensify questions about how well SoftBank will weather setbacks currently buffeting the AI sector.Softbank has invested heavily in AI – spanning from data centres to robotics as well as the $64.6 billion ⁠purchase of a 13% stake in ChatGPT maker OpenAI . However, the company’s high AI borrowing has become a concern for some investors as its financing costs jumped to 462 billion yen in the quarter.
Article Summary: Softbank has reported a $7 billion quarterly loss because of hefty buildout costs for data centres in the US. The Japanese investment giant raised $56.5 billion during the July-September quarter, its highest ever quarterly total. The company said it logged a $3.7 billion loss due to advance payments for equipment in US data centre projects.

Article Title: California defeats what was being regarded as biggest of test of taxing billionaires' wealth in America and why its failure is a win for Democratic leaders
Article Text:
What Prop 40 would have done

Win for California Governor Gavin Newsom and establishment Democrats

Billionaires and tech leaders poured millions into opposition campaign

Supporters framed tax as healthcare funding solution

Younger voters backed measure, older voters opposed it

Opposition extended beyond business groups

Debate far from over

California voters have rejected Proposition 40, a first-in-the-nation ballot measure that would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of residents worth more than $1 billion, dealing a significant blow to progressive efforts to tax concentrated wealth and handing a political victory to Democratic leaders who opposed the proposal. The Associated Press projected the measure's defeat after enough votes had been counted to determine that the "no" campaign had prevailed. The result marks the most significant test yet of a wealth tax in the United States, an idea long championed by progressive politicians as a way to raise revenue from the ultra-rich by taxing their investment wealth rather than only their income.If imposed Prop 40 would lead to imposition of a one-time 5% tax on the wealth of Californians with a net worth above $1 billion. It is said that most of the money collected would have backfilled federal cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone to education and food-assistance programs. SEIU United Healthcare Workers West, who supported the tax, said that it was needed to replace the estimated $100 billion the state will lose in federal healthcare funding over five years. As per the report by Associated Press Prop 40 was said to be the nation’s biggest test yer of an idea progressives have long championed: taxing the ultra-rich on their investments, the main source of their wealth, rather than on paychecks.The failure of Proposition 40 is seen as a victory for California Governor Gavin Newsom and other Democratic leaders who argued that a state-level wealth tax could damage California's economy and drive wealthy residents to relocate. The outcome could also carry broader political implications for Newsom, who is widely viewed as a potential contender in the 2028 US presidential race. While the governor has supported a national minimum tax on individuals with net worth exceeding $100 million, he strongly opposed implementing a wealth tax at the state level, arguing that California would be put at a competitive disadvantage. The defeat also shields Democratic leaders from concerns that the measure could destabilise a state budget already heavily dependent on tax payments from its highest earners.The campaign against Proposition 40 significantly outspent supporters. According to the AP report, opponents raised roughly 10 times more money than the measure's backers. A political action committee called Building a Better California, which opposed the proposal and backed related measures aimed at neutralising its effects, raised more than $333 million. Google co-founder Sergey Brin alone contributed more than $100 million, making him one of the campaign's most prominent financial backers.The measure also prompted some of Silicon Valley's most influential figures to reassess their ties to California. Brin and fellow Google co-founder Larry Page were among billionaires who reportedly began distancing themselves from the state ahead of the vote. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, meanwhile, had previously indicated he would remain in California and arranged financial mechanisms to help cover any potential tax liability without reducing his ownership stake in the company.Backers of Proposition 40 argued that the wealth tax was necessary to help offset an estimated $100 billion reduction in federal healthcare funding that California is projected to lose over five years. Under the proposal, most proceeds from the tax would have gone toward replacing healthcare funding shortfalls, while 10% would have been directed to education and food-assistance programmes.The effort was led by SEIU United Healthcare Workers West and attracted support from progressive national figures including Senator Bernie Sanders, who campaigned across California in the final weeks before voting concluded. Supporters argued that the proposal was designed to protect healthcare services rather than punish wealth, but they struggled to overcome concerns about its economic consequences and the massive financial advantage enjoyed by opponents.According to the AP Voter Poll, support for Proposition 40 was strongest among younger Californians. Most voters under the age of 30 supported the measure, while roughly seven in ten voters aged 65 and older opposed it. Income levels also played a role in voting patterns. About half of voters with household incomes below $100,000 annually supported the initiative, while nearly six in ten voters earning $100,000 or more opposed it. The divide highlighted differing views among Californians on how aggressively governments should tax extreme wealth to fund public services.Notably, opposition to the measure was not limited to business interests and wealthy donors. Several traditional Democratic allies, including Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association, joined a coalition opposing Proposition 40. The groups said they were concerned about how the tax revenues would be allocated and warned that the proposal risked triggering an exodus of wealthy taxpayers whose income taxes contribute substantially to California's budget.Critics characterised the proposal as an economic experiment that carried significant fiscal risks for the state.Although voters rejected the measure, supporters have signalled that the fight over taxing billionaire wealth is far from settled. Campaign organisers said they could return with a similar proposal in 2028 if healthcare funding concerns persist. "The billionaires may have bought themselves a temporary victory at the ballot box, but they have not bought themselves an end to this debate," supporters said after the result became clear.
Article Summary: Prop 40 would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of Californians worth more than $1 billion. It is said that most of the money collected would have backfilled federal cuts to healthcare, and 10% would have gone to education and food-assistance programs. Supporters argued that the proposal was designed to protect healthcare services rather than punish wealth, but they struggled to overcome concerns about its economic consequences.

Article Title: Meta: Days before he got an offer from Meta, to lead the company's AI lab, Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a 'long note' whose first principle was that he does not need a lot of people, as what mat
Article Text:
Cheeky Pint

A 44-minute call that led to a major hire

Why Mark Zuckerberg chose Alexandr Wang

A ‘supernova’ recruiting push

The results and the stakes

Days before accepting an offer to lead Meta’s artificial intelligence efforts, Meta’s AI chief Alexandr Wang sent Mark Zuckerberg a lengthy memo outlining how he would approach the company’s AI ambitions. According to a Fortune report, the first principle in that note was simple: success in AI is not about having the largest workforce, but about having the highest concentration of top talent. Wang, the 29-year-old co-founder of Scale AI who now heads Meta Superintelligence Labs, revealed details of the memo during an appearance alongside Zuckerberg on thepodcast hosted by Stripe co-founder John Collison. The discussion offered a rare glimpse into the conversations that preceded one of the biggest executive hires in the AI industry.The partnership began taking shape in April 2025, shortly after Meta’s Llama 4 models received a lukewarm response. Wang recalled receiving a WhatsApp message from Zuckerberg asking whether he had time for a call. That conversation lasted about 44 minutes.Two days later, Wang sent Zuckerberg a detailed memo describing what he would do if he were running Meta’s AI division. Recalling the advice, Zuckerberg said the very first principle centred on “talent density.”“The very first thing is that you don’t need a lot of people, and talent density is the thing that matters,” Zuckerberg said. According to the Meta CEO, the second principle was being willing to rebuild from scratch. Zuckerberg acknowledged that the company was unhappy with the direction of Llama 4 and was prepared to reorganise its AI efforts if necessary.The decision to put Wang in charge of Meta’s AI ambitions surprised some observers because the entrepreneur had built Scale AI into a data-labelling giant but had never personally led the training of a frontier AI model. Zuckerberg, however, said he had admired Wang for years and viewed him as one of the sharpest entrepreneurs of his generation. Before making the decision, he spoke with leaders across major AI research labs but remained convinced that Wang was the right person for the role. “I talked to like all the leaders of all the labs, like all the heads of research,” Zuckerberg said on the podcast. “And I was like, no, Alex is the guy.”Zuckerberg described what followed as a “supernova” recruiting effort. Meta paid $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Scale AI to bring Wang aboard and reportedly offered $100 million pay packages to OpenAI researchers. Zuckerberg cleared his calendar for two months, and he said neither of them slept much in the first couple of months. Meta’s core research team in the lab has fewer than 200 people, and Wang said it is closer to 100. It is backed by larger infrastructure and product teams at a company of about 75,000 employees. Wang said he built a culture of “insecure overachievers.”The lab’s first model, Muse Spark, arrived in April. On Monday, Meta released Muse Wonder, the first model from the lab it calls frontier-class. Wang said it is state-of-the-art on his team’s measurements for personal and professional agent tasks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, the flagship version lands roughly level with leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic but a couple of points behind the leader, according to AI Weekly.The Muse app launched in the US on September 8 and quickly became the most popular free app in Apple’s App Store. It topped 2.5 million downloads in about two weeks, according to Sensor Tower data cited by CNN. Zuckerberg said late last year that Meta was discussing spending as much as $100 billion or $200 billion, and recalled asking Wang whether he was sure it would work. Wang said Meta CFO Susan Li pulled him aside at an executive gathering in Hawaii to stress that the model has to work, because failure would be very bad in financial terms. Meta expects 2026 capital spending of $130 billion to $145 billion, nearly double last year’s $72.2 billion.Wang also praised Zuckerberg’s leadership, saying he has fully internalised power laws. Once Zuckerberg adopts a belief, Wang said, the speed and scale at which he will change earlier decisions are unusual.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, 29, is the co-founder of Scale AI and now heads Meta Superintelligence Labs. Mark Zuckerberg called Wang on WhatsApp and asked if he had time for a call. Two days later, Wang sent Zuckerberg a detailed memo describing what he would do if he were running Meta’s AI division. Zuckerberg described what followed as a ‘supernova’ recruiting effort.

Article Title: Chinese AI lab that Dario Amodei complained to the US government is targeting Nvidia' most-powerful chips that are banned in China; and the route the company is taking is Europe
Article Text:
Nvidia

Moonshot AI’s ‘European workaround’

AI companies racing to meet surging demand

Moonshot AI, the Chinese artificial intelligence (AI) lab previously accused by the White House of remotely tapping into advanced Nvidia chips in East Asia, has been looking to secure access to those same restricted processors through European data centers, CNBC has reported. Citing four people familiar with the private discussions, the report said that talks have taken place this year for Moonshot to rent computing capacity from “neoclouds” hosting Nvidia GPUs inside European facilities. Moonshot is the maker of the Kimi AI assistant and in September, the company was accused by Anthropic of unauthorised model distillation and terms-of-service violations by secretly routing user requests through Claude.CNBC reports that Moonshot has been trying to lease capacity powered by Nvidia’s Blackwell systems, the cutting-edge chips that are effectively barred from being imported into China under US export controls. While US export rules block the physical shipment of Nvidia’s most advanced hardware to China, renting them remotely through overseas data centers remains a legal gray area. Current US law does not give regulators broad authority to stop foreign companies from accessing restricted chips via cloud services hosted abroad.To get around the bottleneck in Europe, a Chinese AI firm typically leases capacity from a non-Chinese neocloud or data center operator that is legally allowed to buy the chips.Two sources told the publication that Moonshot was looking to rent European clusters for inference while one source noted the lab was also interested in clusters for model training. Discussions have included deals for Moonshot to access clusters of 8,000 or more Blackwell GPUs in the region. One source described the lab as “very aggressive” in its hunt for computing power, adding that talks in Europe have continued even after the White House accused Moonshot in July of accessing Blackwell chips through a facility in Thailand.Founded in 2023, Beijing-based Moonshot AI is one of China’s premier model builders, known for its Kimi family of AI models. In July, the company released a new model that it claimed closed the performance gap with leading systems from US rivals like OpenAI and Anthropic.Lower costs and improved capabilities have fueled a surge in global adoption for Chinese AI models throughout 2026. Around the launch of Kimi K3, demand grew so intense that Moonshot temporarily paused new subscriptions to protect computing power for existing users.“We’re adding capacity as fast as we can and will reopen new subscription spots in batches,” the company wrote in a LinkedIn post at the time.Meanwhile, the Financial Times reported last week that Nvidia has instructed cloud providers selling access to its chips that at least 51% of their services must go to non-Chinese customers. Responding to those reports, an Nvidia spokesperson said: “America cannot win the AI race unless America’s AI infrastructure wins worldwide — if the world’s clouds rely on foreign-made chips, the model and application layers will be foreign-built as well. ”
Article Summary: Moonshot AI has been looking to secure access to restricted processors through European data centers, CNBC has reported. Talks have taken place this year for Moonshot to rent computing capacity from “neoclouds” hosting Nvidia GPUs inside European facilities.

Article Title: Months before Marco Rubio's memo to the US government, how an year-old report 'warned' America on Alice Huang and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as it called 'mystery lady CEO and billions in sales' to ...
Article Text:
Jensen Huang with Alice Huang

What Rubio’s memo reportedly said

How Megaspeed got the chips

Poll Vote & Share your view What action should Nvidia take in response to the allegations against Megaspeed? Increase transparency Conduct a thorough investigation 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Nvidia’s link to Singapore’s Megaspeed is getting awkward. Before US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged ties to a Chinese businesswoman, the New York Times had already rung the warning bells. Months before Nvidia launched its own independent investigation, the publication reported that the American intelligence agencies already suspected that the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security and used her company to import banned Nvidia chips in mainland China. Megaspeed is the Singapore-based firm where Alice Huang is a senior executive, and the company has reportedly spent billions of dollars in Nvidia chip purchases.According to a report by The NYT, Rubio oversaw a highly classified memo that circulated among senior administration officials in May. It warned that Jensen Huang had built a close relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen and senior executive at Megaspeed. The memo was based on intelligence gathered through electronic surveillance of Alice Huang. People briefed on the matter said the memo was shared with officials holding high-level security clearances ahead of Trump’s China trip in May.US officials suspected Megaspeed of illegally smuggling restricted Nvidia semiconductors into mainland China.However, an October 2025 report by the publication already red-flagged this, claiming that Commerce Department officials had been investigating whether Megaspeed – which has close ties to Chinese tech firms – is helping companies in China sidestep American export restrictions. The report says more than a half dozen current and former officials and others familiar with the companies said so, on condition of anonymity, because the examination is not public.The earlier report had described a scene from a humid June night the year before. Jensen Huang was holding court with several of Nvidia’s major Asian customers at a bar with sweeping views of Taipei. They stood and toasted the booming AI industry. Next to him stood Huang Le, also known as Alice Huang, a Megaspeed executive. Her company was poised to buy $2 billion of Nvidia AI technology over the next year. She and Megaspeed were little-known players in the AI industry, but their link to Nvidia and its chief had become a preoccupation in Washington.Not just US but Singapore police were also investigating Megaspeed for breaching local laws. The inquiry raises questions about how closely Nvidia tracks where its AI chips end up. It also highlights how easily American export laws might be sidestepped.Megaspeed split off from a Chinese gaming company in 2023. It then set up a subsidiary in Malaysia that quickly bought nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia’s most advanced products. Citing records from the trade data platform ImportGenius, most of those chips came from the US branch of a Chinese company that has already been sanctioned for providing technology to the Chinese military.Megaspeed has sent those chips to data centres in Malaysia and Indonesia that appear to serve customers in China remotely. That is not necessarily illegal, but it can be unlawful if done on behalf of a Chinese company.Another report from The New York Times, published last month, claimed that when US officials told Trump about a Chinese spy plot, he took no action. Reason: the report explains that the US was already leading China in the AI race and Trump did not want to ‘disrupt’ Nvidia’s chip sales, which were helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.Notably, none of the spying claims have been proven, and Nvidia’s board says it has no reason to believe national security or its trade secrets were compromised.
Article Summary: US officials suspected Megaspeed of illegally smuggling restricted Nvidia semiconductors into mainland China. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned senior Trump administration officials about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged ties to a Chinese businesswoman. The New York Times had already rung the warning bells months before Nvidia launched its own independent investigation.

We are aware of the recent article published by Bloomberg which has raised concerns regarding our operations.

We would like to clarify that the article contains misleading information and incorrect insinuations, including suggestions that we may have been involved in illegal chip transfers.

We want to be absolutely clear: over the past six months, our company has undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews by key institutions, including the Bureau of Industry and Security of the U.S. Commerce Department, the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry of Malaysia, and NVIDIA.

These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities, and this demonstrates that we are a compliant and legitimate company.

We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.

Our company has always adhered to the law, and we take these accusations seriously. As such, we do not rule out pursuing legal action to protect our reputation and to hold Bloomberg accountable for the misleading nature of the article.

We appreciate the continued trust and support from our clients and partners.

Megaspeed December 23, 2025

Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed, which has recently come under renewed attention following reports about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair with one of its executives, continues to stand by a statement it first issued nearly 10 months ago denying allegations that it was involved in illegally transferring Nvidia chips to China. The statement, dated December 23, 2025, was released after a Bloomberg report raised questions about Megaspeed's operations and suggested the company may have played a role in moving restricted AI chips into China. The company rejected the allegations, describing the report as containing "misleading information and incorrect insinuations."In its official response, Megaspeed said there was "no evidence" that it had violated export-control rules or engaged in illicit transfers of advanced semiconductors. The company said it had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews over a six-month period by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), Malaysia's Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry, and Nvidia itself."These thorough investigations have confirmed that there has been no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities," the company said in the statement.Megaspeed added that it operates in compliance with all applicable export-control regulations and maintains "the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct."The Singapore-based firm also signalled that it could pursue legal remedies over the reporting."Our company has always adhered to the law, and we take these accusations seriously. As such, we do not rule out pursuing legal action to protect our reputation and to hold Bloomberg accountable for the misleading nature of the article," the statement said. The company concluded by thanking customers and partners for their support.The New York Times reported on October 29 that US intelligence agencies believed Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese citizen and senior Megaspeed executive, was passing information to Beijing. She is not related to Jensen Huang. According to the report, surveillance of her as part of the chip-smuggling investigation revealed her close relationship with the Nvidia chief. The Commerce Department investigation, which began in late 2024, was later handed to the Justice Department, the Times reported. China’s embassy has called the allegations groundless smears.Nvidia opened an investigation into Jensen Huang on Sunday after he acknowledged to the company that he had been intimate with Alice Huang. The company said it has no reason to believe national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised. Nvidia has said claims that Megaspeed diverted chips to China were “thoroughly investigated and debunked last year.” Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said Alice Huang was not investigated over alleged ties to China, though authorities there have confirmed a domestic investigation into Megaspeed over corporate fraud and supplier misrepresentation, according to WION.
Article Summary: Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed stands by statement it issued nearly 10 months ago denying allegations it was involved in illegally transferring Nvidia chips to China. The company said it had undergone multiple on-site inspections and reviews over a six-month period by the US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security.
